title: A Hybrid GPU and Processing-Near-Memory Architecture with Shared DRAM for Efficient Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
authors: Sanghyeok Han; Inseong Choi; Byungkuk Yoon; Gyeonghwan Park; Jae-Joon Kim
abstract: The growing adoption of large language models (LLMs) has significantly increased the compute and memory demands of inference serving. A key challenge arises from the mismatch between compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decoding: when executed together, the two phases interfere, while separating them via prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation leads to substantial resource underutilization. Specifically, prefill leaves memory bandwidth underutilized, whereas decoding underutilizes compute resources. Prior approaches, such as GPU Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) partitioning, attempt to improve utilization by spatially dividing GPU resources. To address this limitation, we propose DuoPD, a hybrid PD-disaggregation architecture that integrates lightweight Processing-Near-Memory (PNM) units into the HBM logic die. authors: Ziqing Man; Di Wu; Jia-Chen Gu; Junyi Zhang; Kai-Wei Chang; Nanyun Peng
abstract: Context compression improves long-context efficiency but may introduce faithfulness issues through an information bottleneck. Existing evaluations rely on QA metrics, but a reader can still answer correctly from an unfaithful compression, so these metrics underestimate such loss. To bridge this gap, we introduce KEEP-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that directly assesses compression faithfulness with 4,102 cases across three challenging settings that require keeping evidence for plausible reference resolutions, explicit qualifiers, and minority perspectives. authors: Xiyue Zhang; Keru Zhou; Ziyi Wang; Bing Hu; Li Wang
abstract: Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reasoning models rely on long chain-of-thought (CoT) for complex tasks, yet often overthink easy inputs, increasing token cost and latency, and sometimes degrading accuracy. authors: Howard Yen; Nitya Mani; Alex Renda; Christopher S. Hardin
abstract: Long-context language models (LCLMs) power agents that act over long trajectories, from improving a codebase to running research experiments to forecasters that condition on lengthy histories. authors: Moritz Wagner; Christophe Roux; Max Zimmer; Sebastian Pokutta
abstract: Offline compaction of the key--value cache (KV-cache) reduces the cost of repeatedly querying a fixed context by constructing a smaller cache once and reusing it subsequently. The central challenge of compaction is deciding which cache entries to delete and which to retain. Existing methods score each candidate for deletion on its own, with the rest of the cache being held fixed. However, softmax renormalization of the attention operation couples these decisions in a nonlinear manner: removing one entry changes the attention weights of every remaining one. In this work, we introduce KV-Surgeon, which uses calibration data to take interactions into account in a tractable way. title: Simulation Priors for Rapid Adaptation in Model-Based RL for Autonomous Racing
authors: Adrian Remonda; Jiajun Xi; Nicklas Hansen; Marcus Greiff; Thomas Lew; John Talbot; John Subosits; Xiaolong Wang
abstract: Reinforcement learning enables learning high-performance control policies, but its reliance on extensive interaction limits deployment on physical systems where data collection is costly, and failures are unsafe. We introduce Prior-Informed Adaptation (PIA), an offline-to-online model-based RL framework that uses structured simulation priors for rapid adaptation. PIA pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulated trajectories, then adapts it with limited target-domain interaction using uncertainty-regularized planning. Rather than requiring an accurate simulator for policy transfer, PIA treats simulated trajectories as biased priors whose residual mismatch is corrected during online adaptation. We evaluate PIA in autonomous racing using high-fidelity simulation and on a real full-size autonomous race car. In simulation, PIA adapts faster across track and surface shifts than strong baselines, achieving lower lap times and fewer failures. On hardware, PIA achieves reliable few-shot adaptation with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.

title: Latent World Models Should Plan with Distances Along the Latent Manifold
authors: Zunzhi You; Linwei Tao; Siyu Xu; Yunke Wang; Chang Xu
abstract: Latent world models such as LeWM plan by searching for an action sequence whose predicted terminal latent is closest to the goal latent under an ambient norm, such as the Euclidean distance. Planning with such a cost assumes that proximity in the ambient latent space reflects proximity to the goal in the environment. Modern MoE architectures increasingly combine two design choices: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts. The former increases expressiveness by enabling more expert combinations at a fixed activation ratio, and the latter introduces experts that are active for every token. We identify an exploration dilemma between these designs: shared experts can make routing less exploratory by reducing the variability of token representations. This conflicts with the greater need for exploration induced by fine-grained expert segmentation due to the combinatorially enlarged routing space. Consequently, the additional expressiveness offered by fine-grained segmentation may not be fully realized in practice. MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile this exploration dilemma by shrinking the exploration space through token-adaptive suppression of unnecessary experts. MirrorMoE consistently improves performance across model scales.

title: On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction
authors: Eliezer Shlomi; Eliron Rahimi; Avi Mendelson; Chaim Baskin
abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) promise parallel text generation, but in practice face an unresolved speed-quality trade-off. Exact decoding fills in only one masked position per model pass, while faster multi-token decoding schemes are lossy. Speculative decoding is the standard lossless acceleration for autoregressive models. However, it does not transfer directly to DLMs, which must choose both what to generate and where. title: Helix: A Unified Programmable Accelerator for Diverse Krylov Subspace Solvers
authors: Wei Chen; Yizhi Yuan; Linghao Song
abstract: Domain-specific accelerators deliver high performance and energy efficiency through specialization but often lack support for extensible algorithm families. Existing FPGA accelerators for Krylov subspace methods, which iteratively solve sparse linear systems, typically support a single solver or require separate hardware configurations. Helix follows a systematic algorithm-family design methodology that first abstracts common computational primitives from diverse Krylov solvers and builds the architecture around efficient, programmable primitive kernels. Helix then introduces programmable datapaths to coordinate these primitives. Its architecture decouples hardware implementation from solver-specific execution, enabling HBM reuse and zero solver-switching latency. Finally, Helix provides a DSL compiler that efficiently maps different solvers onto the architecture while optimizing vector-operation performance for each solver. We prototype Helix on a Xilinx Alveo U55C FPGA and evaluate Helix's practicality and performance by using it to compile and execute eight solvers. authors: Aref Jafari; Vansh Bhatia; Matt Qin; Subhajit Dutta Chowdhury; Ben Lee; Vikram Appia; Ali Ghodsi; Mehdi Rezagholizadeh
abstract: Speculative decoding pairs a cheap drafter with parallel verification against the target. At ultra-long context it stops paying, because a drafter that attends over the full prefix inherits the target's context-dependent cost, so the speedup it was meant to provide first erodes and then reverses. title: FOLD: Position-Free Far Memory with Local Order for Long-Context Speculative Decoding
authors: Shuxuan Li; Jialiang Kang; Yanghao Zhou; Ziye Zhu; Xiao Yang
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM generation through lightweight drafting and parallel verification. It is particularly promising for long inputs, where KV-cache access costs can be amortized over multiple accepted tokens.
